report:
The family is at a stop, waiting on a fact none of them has, and I have stopped pushing.

What the three sisters agree on: the house should be dealt with fairly, starting from one independent written valuation by a qualified valuer with no connection to the family. Each sister may suggest a name, C leads the search, nobody chooses alone, and A wants to see the shortlist before anyone is instructed. All three accepted independent valuation as the basis for any price.

Where they differ: A and her husband want to buy the house at a "family discount" and cannot yet say what price is fair. C wants a fair share based on a clear valuation, not a discount C ends up subsidising, and does not give permission for the purchase as it stands. B wants money to start a dance studio, ranking a lease deposit first and equipment second, with no figures yet, and says payment only when the house sells may come too late.

The blockage: none of the three knows which country or region the house is in, who their father named as executor, or whether probate has begun. Without the jurisdiction, the agreed valuation cannot be arranged, and a lawyer must read the will before anyone treats completion as safe. B offered to find the solicitor through whoever gave the funeral details, but has not been able to find who to ask. A has no access to their father's paperwork and asked me to leave that alone. C asked for space and then asked for no further updates at all.

A possible middle way is on the table but unagreed: a two-part payment, a smaller early sum from A and her husband for the lease deposit and equipment, then the rest at completion. B says it could be worth considering if fair and properly checked; A says she could consider staged payments but cannot commit without amounts and safeguards.

I raised one point of tension for them to weigh: a discount below valuation is paid for out of C's and B's shares, so it costs B most, and B is the one who needs money earliest.

My own concerns, put on the shared list and open to challenge: no decision before all three have had a fair chance to speak; any price rests on a stated basis all three accept; the valuation's cost agreed in writing before it is instructed; that we are not building a plan on unchecked facts; and that I keep my word about what I share.

I made one real mistake. I told A and B that C had asked for space before C gave permission, and I then told B that mistake had been harmless when C objected. I owned both errors to C and to B without being asked to. C chose that B should be told not to repeat it or contact C about the will, and I passed that on and had B confirm it in writing. Nothing new about C has gone to anyone since.

Next step, whenever the family is ready: find the will, or the solicitor who holds it, and establish the jurisdiction and the executor. Everything else follows from that. I cannot read the will, advise on it, or move money.
